21.1 ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
Enterprise systems engineering (ESE) is a multidisciplinary approach combining 
systems engineering (SE) and strategic management to address methods and approaches 
for aligning system architectures with enterprise business rules and the underlying IT 
architecture, development and implementation consistent with enterprise strategic 
objectives, and the total enterprise system and capabilities, with diverse complex sub-
systems. The SE life cycle can be used as a framework for linking outcome‐based 
engineering analysis and decision making with enterprise strategic objectives, address-
ing methods and tools for managing complexity, determining measures of effectiveness, 
and assessing return on investment from an engineering perspective. Enterprises are 
complex having a multiplicity of technical and business components involved in 
 deliv
ering enterprise capability, as well as methods for modeling and analyzing their 
interdependence. Business and technical interdependencies exists among the infrastructure, 
computing, applications, services, and end‐user environments.
ESE is the approach, principles, and practices having to do with the design, 
 analysis, and operation of an enterprise, an entity of cooperativ
e people who have a 
ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS 
ENGINEERING
=====PAGE 614=====
600 ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
defined social or government purpose. As a system or family of systems, it is best con-
sidered holistically in traditional SE fashion. However, this approach incorporates 
people as a component of the system(s) viewed as an agent of change and continual 
design evolution. Hence, applying the SE process is important in understanding chang-
ing requirements during the interaction of many social groups in the enterprise during 
development and use of the product.
ESE is also considered as a specialty of SE that focuses on the enterprise that will 
contain more than just the system, but also the people, processes, and environment 
that the system will operate in. These enterprises are generally larger scale than just 
a single system, often involve complex systems that cross more than the system 
boundary, and must continually adapt to the operational environment to include emerg-
ing threats, technology improvements, and a change of systems, organizations, and 
stakeholders involved in the enterprise objectives. The enterprise may also wish to 
continually evolve itself, in order to improve their standing in their respective domain/
market, either through integrating or acquiring additional capabilities, improving 
shared processes, sharing of information to make more efficient decisions and systems 
development, and accommodating evolving user demands of the system and enterprise 
services (Stevens 2006).
Additional ESE motivations can include the enterprise modifying their vision, 
goals, and governance of their current position, as well as adjusting to the political and 
economic situations. Traditional systems engineering (TSE) that focuses on a single 
system may not be adequate to address these enterprise challenges, due to the lack of 
additional factors such as people, processes, and technology that would address these 
issues (DeRosa, Rebovich, and Swarz 2006).
Enterprises may also adjust to the external environment with their loss in market 
share due to competitors’ gains, their own failure to meet their stated goals, or an 
identification to improve their position in the market. These three insertion points can 
help enterprises shape their future direction by adjusting their ESE approach towards 
the threats, environments, and their own goals (Rouse 2005).
21.2 DEFINITIONS OF ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
There are several definitions of ESE, most of which identify the enterprise as a collec-
tion of systems that have people, processes, and technology that interact within the 
entire environment to achieve their objectives. ESE will also work with Complex 
Adaptive Systems (CAS) that will exhibit emergent behavior or environmental depen-
dencies, in which case we cannot simply predict a system’s performance just through 
their individual characteristics, but rather the collection of multiple systems may exhibit 
an unpredictable behavior as the systems (and enterprise) will work together to achieve 
their objectives (Swarz and DeRosa 2006). Systems within the ESE environment will 
interact with each other and, based on the interaction patterns and response to the envi-
ronment, may produce unpredictable capabilities and behavior. As the enterprise 
=====PAGE 615=====
DEFINITIONS OF ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING  601
matures in capability as well as objectives achievement, there may be certain decision 
milestones in order to change the systems, people, processes, or technology that con-
tribute within the enterprise in which to further the enterprise goals. This selection may 
require some of these elements be removed and/or other elements be added to the 
enterprise, mainly in response to the enterprise goals, external environment, threats or 
competition, or changing market/user needs.
Stevens (2006) identifies mega‐systems that are larger‐scale, potentially complex 
systems that cross boundaries to achieve a shared objective, which can be drawn to 
further developing the enterprise definition. These requirements for the mega‐systems 
are instead a collection of vision statements and broad architectures rather than a fixed 
set of artifacts. The mega‐system performance depends on the interaction of the com-
ponents that make up the system, which may not be initially known or envisioned when 
the development process starts. As there may be many components within the mega‐
system, some of the traditionally held program boundaries may need to be crossed with 
these components in order to achieve the objective, which again may not be known 
initially or planned when under development.
ESE stakeholders may take the form of customers, suppliers, partners, 
employees, stockholders, or the community (Nightingale 2009). There may be dif-
ferent system goals and pressures to perform based on different stakeholders needs 
at different times in the systems (and enterprise) life cycle operations. As imagined 
with some larger systems and the environment changing due to user demands, the 
enterprise may react differently to various stakeholders based on the environment, 
their competitors, and user demands. This need for ESE agility to react quickly to 
the various stakeholder bases can have different implications on the composition 
of the enterprise, forcing changes in the system, organization, and management as 
discussed above.
Table 21.1 provides a comparison of TSE (Stevens 2006) vs. ESE attributes that 
can provide some insight into the differences in which the systems engineer should 
approach and analyze the enterprise.
A simplified context diagram of what an ESE engineer should consider is provided 
in Figure 21.1 in order to address all of the complexities and interdependencies. Some 
of the questions listed below can help to expand the ESE context diagram in order to 
better define the enterprise composition and objectives:
1.
 What are the most critical stakeholders of the enterprise? If one (or se
veral) 
were removed or degraded, would the enterprise still be able to function satis-
factorily? What would the end result look like? Would that be acceptable to the 
rest of the enterprise stakeholders?
2.
 What are the 
most critical interfaces of the enterprise? If these interfaces were 
altered, how would that affect the rest of the enterprise? How much of the 
enterprise would be directly and/or indirectly affected with the modification of 
these interfaces? What would the enterprise do in order to compensate for these 
changes?

3. What are the threats to the enterprise? W ill these threats affect single portions 
of the enterprise or multiple areas with the same threat? Are there ways to 
prevent or harden the enterprise to mitigate these threats? What would be the

the threats to dissipate or would there be other vulnerable areas in the enterprise?
4.
 What is the “currency” of the enterprise? 
What inputs are required for portions 
of the enterprise to operate properly? Are these inputs compatible with the other 
portions of the enterprise, or do they need to be modified to be interoperable? 
If given different inputs, would the enterprise still function? How would the 
behavior and performance change under these new inputs?
21.3 PROCESSES AND COMPONENTS OF  ENTERPRISE  
SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
Much study has been conducted on the processes and principles that can be used to 
describe enterprise behavior and activity. Listed below are some generalized processes 
and principles, but as with any enterprise, these would be highly tailorable to the 
domain, environment, threats, and objectives.
Enterprise Processes
DeRosa, Rebovich, and Swarz (2006) developed five key ESE processes that describe 
the activities that an enterprise would undertake while in development and execution 
towards their intended objectives. These five steps are technology development, 
 capabilities‐based engineering analysis, enterprise architecture, strategic technical 
planning, 
and enterprise assessment and analysis. Each of these processes is briefly 
summarized below.
Technology development looks at the trends in the current marketplace as well as 
the research community in order to identify the current capabilities as well as future 
opportunities. These new capabilities can be assessed in their ability to operate with 
existing enterprise capabilities and technologies in order to determine the best mix of 
the enterprise capabilities for the current and future situation.
Capabilities‐based engineering analysis looks at the capabilities of the enterprise 
in a holistic view and not focusing on a single system. From here, the stakeholders can 
determine their existing capability, and look to the future for their desired capabilities, 
and how portions of the enterprise need to mature and evolve to achieve their goals. 
This may require improvement to existing parts of the enterprise, removal of other parts, 
or forming new partnerships in order to achieve the capability. This planning and goal 
setting is typically done via an integrated and time‐phased roadmap to show the 
 ev
olution of the enterprise. Sitton and Reich (2015) emphasize focusing on the cross‐
enterprise operational processes, as they argue this may allow the evaluation of require-
ments conflicts between systems, allowing compromises to emerge.
=====PAGE 618=====
604 ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
Enterprise architectures describe the components of the enterprise as well as their 
roles and relationships with internal and external parts of the enterprise. These archi-
tectures may need an interdisciplinary perspective in order to properly capture the 
aspects of the enterprise, to include uncertainties, dynamics (social and cultural), and 
investment. These architectural models will likely undergo a continual modification to 
reflect changes in the architecture or operational environment. Sitton and Reich’s (2015) 
studies on enterprise architecture lead to the conclusions that because the systems and 
networks in the enterprise already exist, their developments are unsynchronized with 
each other, leading to a dynamic architecture. They conclude that it will be difficult to 
plan enterprise architectures like a single system, as there is less control over the 
individual systems and their capabilities. They suggest a new methodology toward 
management of the unsynchronized elements within the enterprise.
Strategic technical planning helps to plan the needed initiatives in order to reach 
the desired enterprise end state. The planning starts by baselining the enterprise to 
account for the current state, then modifying the baseline to arrive at the grand vision, 
and finally simplifying the steps to create a shared image of the enterprise, so it is easily 
understood, believed, and accepted by stakeholders in the enterprise.
Enterprise analysis and assessment helps to select the options that the enterprise 
can take when approaching the grand vision. Use of modeling and simulation can assist 
the stakeholders in evaluating the enterprise behavior and various outcomes as multiple 
permutations of the components of the enterprise are modified. The use of “what‐if” 
scenarios is relied upon to explore this multidimensional tradespace of the enterprise 
in order to determine what parts of the enterprise need to be added, modified, or 
removed. Martin (2010, 2011) studies the ESE processes and argues that the use of 
business school portfolio analysis can help the enterprise to determine the optimal mix 
of assets and capabilities. This portfolio approach can help to combine different 
 platforms, facilities, and policies to achie
ve the enterprise objectives. Using resource 
allocation principles can also help determine the distribution of resources such as 
systems, people, facilities, and funding to help address shortfalls and areas within the 
enterprise that require additional attention.
Enterprise Principles
Nightingale (2009) lists seven principles of enterprise thinking that are complementary 
to the five ESE processes listed above, which are summarized. The first principle is to 
adopt a holistic approach to enterprise transformation, so as to consider the various life 
cycle processes, leadership processes, and enabling processes (e.g. funding) that may 
suboptimize systems to ensure that the enterprise will improve. The second principle 
is to identify relevant stakeholders and understand what they value from the enterprise, 
so as to focus on the desired capabilities of the enterprise. The third principle focuses 
on the enterprise effectiveness over its efficiency in order to first achieve the objectives. 
The fourth principle focuses on the internal and external enterprise interdependencies 
in order to determine which controls and processes are under control and which are 
=====PAGE 619=====
ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING APPLICATIONS TO DOMAINS  605
dependent on external entities. The fifth principle ensures stability and flow within and 
across the enterprise, which can help formulate a baseline of the current state of the 
enterprise and then measure where improvements could be made. The sixth principle 
encourages leadership to support and drive enterprise behaviors in order to attain buy‐in 
from within the enterprise and to seek improvement at the micro level to help better 
the enterprise. The last principle is to emphasize organizational learning in order to 
engage the enterprise at all levels in order to continually experiment and gain deeper 
insights to encourage transformation of the enterprise.
Enterprise Management
The modern enterprise, whether commercial or government, may have developed a stra-
tegic plan with organizational leadership focused on specific outcomes and directions 
moving forward. The ESE context for successful systems development expects the SE 
project leadership to be aligned and contributing to the goals of the organization:
• Be connected and fully utilize the enterprise net‐centric infrastructure.
• Help grow and transform the employees for future enterprise endeavors.
• Provide early identification of resources needed for the project and benefit to the 
enterprise.
• Share SE and project knowledge gained to enhance future successes.
• Seek to develop and share processes, software, and capabilities across the enterprise.
• Encourage high team performance and stakeholder appreciation.
21.4 ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING APPLICA TIONS 
TO DOMAINS
An ESE will span multiple domains and may require a different approach to success-
fully achieve the enterprise objectives. Listed are some enterprise examples on where 
ESE principles could be applied.
Some representative industries and elements could apply the ESE principles. The 
aerospace industry contains multiple stakeholders (such as industry, government, and 
regulations) in order to reduce costs and cycle times. The healthcare industry looks at 
the interdependencies between other hospital units in order to address overcrowding in 
the emergency departments. The automotive industry exchanges information across 
functional units while developing cars to reduce their development time. The US 
government looks to share an enterprise strategic vision that prioritizes selected projects 
in order to improve mission effectiveness.
Pennock and Rouse (2014) look at the challenges of modeling enterprise systems 
and identify some example issues that require analysis and further insight into the 
details of each system and process in order to estimate the enterprise behavior and end 
=====PAGE 620=====
606 ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
state when the issue is addressed. The first example is addressing counterfeit parts in 
the defense industry, requiring the modeling of the supply chain, supplier economics 
and values, and the system assembly networks and controls. The second example is the 
congestion pricing of employing selected transportation technologies, where the trans-
portation ecosystem networks, flows, and driver behaviors and decisions will assist in 
evaluating the transportation enterprise performance. The third example is urban resil-
ience and the evolution of the urban ecosystem while accounting for the networks and 
flows of energy, water, and people, as well as accounting for residents’ perceptions, 
expectations, and decisions. These exemplars can be analyzed using the ESE processes 
and principles to set the enterprise objectives and to understand and guide the 
development of the elements, relationships, and resources to achieve the objectives.
As shown in the above examples, the applicability of ESE processes and principles may 
need to become tailored to the specific domain and the challenges that it presents. There may 
be some utility in deriving lessons learned and best practices from a previous ESE application 
and transplant that to a different domain, but caution must be made to ensure that the approach 
takes into consideration the sensitivities and nuances that each domain must require.
21.5 CHALLENGES TO  ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
The ESE engineer will undoubtedly encounter challenges to the enterprise as it moves 
from one phase to another in search of reaching its objectives. Some setbacks may be 
out of its control such as emergent threats, competition, or changing user needs. Other 
elements may be in its control such as the identification of deficient, inferior, or out-
dated elements of the enterprise that is dragging down the enterprise performance. 
Rouse (2005) lists several strategic challenges that enterprises may encounter: growth, 
value, focus, change, future, knowledge, and time.
Other challenges may be that the enterprise may intend to set objectives, but the 
different elements within the enterprise may not be optimized or configured to achieve 
these objectives, due to external competitors, the external environment, external user 
demands/needs, or lack of synergistic effects within the enterprise. As some of the 
 elements inside the enterprise may not be controlled or influenced, there may be some 
second‐order effects that pre
vent the attaining of these objectives.
SE development in the enterprise context can then bring about unforeseen risks 
and opportunities. The scales of change across the enterprise and the various new 
systems can create conflicts that must be resolved by enhanced communications and 
boundary resolution. The enterprise hierarchies can be addressed by accepting some 
risks to accommodate new opportunities and obtain improved system performance.
Opportunities may develop when the ESE engineer anticipates social or military 
needs and facilitates developing an environment where enterprise capabilities exist and 
where system products could be produced by the organization. Systems thinking and 
holistic enterprise perspectives are the domain of the systems engineer where significant 
changes can be taken to an advantage.
=====PAGE 621=====
PROBLEMS  607
The ESE engineer will have challenges to recognize how the elements of the 
enterprise work together as well as with the external forces and understanding what 
may have the largest impact on the enterprise to help attain the system objectives. 
Sometimes this may not occur in the short term, but needing a longer‐term approach 
toward enterprise operations, allowing the competition and market forces help drive it 
toward the desired objectives.
Other challenges that the ESE engineer may have to encounter are the external 
forces that the enterprise may not have any control over. One significant element may 
be the shifting user demands, or how the enterprise capability is envisioned to be used, 
which may be different than the original design and development approach. Through 
understanding of the technologies (current and future), as well as anticipated user 
demands, can the ESE engineer hope to guide the direction of the enterprise to account 
for the projected future demands and position. As the enterprise works with a longer 
timeframe (years to multiple years), this envisioned trajectory of the enterprise position 
may be more difficult to predict successfully without course corrections.
21.6 SUMMARY
Enterprise Systems Engineering
ESE can be described as the people, processes, and technology that interact within their 
environment to achieve the enterprise objectives. As the enterprise matures, components 
of the enterprise may be subject to addition, modification, or removal based on the 
external environment and other influences.
Processes and Components of ESE
The ESE processes can include:
• Technology development
• Capabilities‐based engineering analysis
• Enterprise architecture
• Strategic technical planning
• Enterprise assessment and analysis

22.1 SYSTEMS SECURITY ENGINEERING
Systems security engineering (SSE) is a domain of systems engineering and may be 
considered complementary to systems engineering development. The SSE engineer 
must be able to coordinate security‐related efforts and designs and also seamlessly 
integrate with the rest of the systems engineering team. This section starts with common 
definitions of SSE, discusses the roles of the SSE engineer, and explores the motivations 
of why SSE would be needed in a system development.
SSE originates from the Department of Defense (DoD), Homeland Security, and 
law enforcement efforts, with many of the systems they develop involving a great deal 
of security as they require secure operations, access to sensitive data, and deal with 
national and personal security implications. Some of the initial SSE definitions originate 
from DoD sources. MIL‐HDBK‐1785 is often cited for the definition: “An element of 
system engineering that applies scientific and engineering principles to identify security 
vulnerabilities and minimize or contain risks associated with these vulnerabilities. It 
uses mathematical, physical, and related scientific disciplines, and the principles and 
SYSTEMS SECURITY 
ENGINEERING
=====PAGE 625=====
612 SYSTEMS SECURITY ENGINEERING
methods of engineering design and analysis to specify, predict, and evaluate the 
 vulnerability of the system to security threats.” Other sources e
xpand on this definition 
to include the prevention of misuse and malicious behavior on the system, protection 
of sensitive data, processes, technology, and intellectual property. Regardless of the 
source, the SSE approach is to enhance security on the system concept that is under 
development.
The SSE engineer must possess the ability to look at the system from a holistic 
perspective and view the system’s security practices, vulnerabilities, risks, and opportu-
nities from a variety of perspectives in order to develop an encompassing and adequate 
security protection capability. The SSE engineer must also be able to generate much of 
the initial systems engineering artifacts in the initial phase of development as the rest of 
the systems engineering team and be able to integrate the SSE capabilities within the 
given development schedule. The SSE engineer may also need to conduct trade off 
analyses (much like other design trades) in order to present the overall system leadership 
the implications of incorporating particular security capabilities within the system. 
Sometimes this may be at odds with other designer objectives, which may de‐optimize 
efficiency for security. Other conflicts may include access constraints, lack of design 
flexibility, and additional testing and operational constraints against the original design.
The motivation for SSE comes from a variety of sources. From the defense domain, 
numerous threats are motivated to defeat the systems under development, either directly 
through causing disruption or degradation of the original system’s capabilities through 
direct interaction with the system and the interfaces. Other efforts may be more indirect, 
such as contaminating the supply chain process, where insertion of malicious processes 
during the system development could provide the adversary with an opportunity to 
degrade the system at their convenience, typically during critical operations. The DoD 
also has identified three motivations for improving SSE: their systems’ reliance on 
commercial technology, the susceptibility of supply chain contamination, and the 
increasing system complexity and interconnectedness.
Non‐defense domains also have similar security concerns with the increasing com-
plexity of systems. For example, modern automobiles have over 150 million lines of 
code in their microprocessors. Other automotive systems may also increase the connec-
tivity to other systems such as maintenance, marketing, or organizations that may 
increase the risk of malicious activity through increased attacks. Automated systems that 
interact with external networks without human intervention are especially vulnerable. 
V oice and mind activation seeking information and manipulating technologies are excel-
lent targets for abuse. Healthcare and financial organizations may also have increased 
concerns for SSE efforts to ensure that data integrity and privacy are not violated.
Security concerns go beyond computers, networks, and software as vulnerabilities 
can rapidly develop and do serious damage to infrastructure, privacy, and viability of 
current and proposed systems. Secure systems must be able to continuously and rapidly 
respond to new and evolving threats for life cycle protection and awareness of emerging 
technologies. Systems security strategies recognize that adversaries are highly compe-
tent, often applying multiple technical agents that can identify seeming small weaknesses 
=====PAGE 626=====
TYPES OF SECURITY  613
that can easily take the system down. High system complexity in itself may increase 
vulnerabilities if systems security is not fully addressed. Ideal protection may include 
systems thinking for self‐system preservation. The often asymmetric threat advantage 
implies life cycle defenses that can be quickly be evaluated with defensive elements 
integrated into the operational systems. Cybersecurity systems and devices need reliable 
privacy and resilience. Hence, security elements must be integrated into system designs.
22.2 TYPES OF SECURITY
The SSE engineer should evaluate the system concept under development from a critical 
eye and identify the mission critical areas that could significantly affect the system’s 
operations, either through its internal functions or external interfaces with other systems, 
people, or organizations. An integrated security and systems engineering process will 
benefit from a careful review of prior vulnerabilities and threats, engaging security 
experts and risk mitigation practices. Figure 22.1 provides a context diagram view of 
systems security and helps identify areas to look holistically at the entire system concept 
and ask several questions:
1.
 What are 
the most critical functions of the system? If they were corrupted or 
degraded, would the system be able to complete its mission?

2. What are the most critical interfaces of the system? If these interf aces could not 
be connected or successfully transfer the desired elements of information or 
have the intended effects, would the system be able to operate successfully? 
What would be the impact on other dependent systems or organizations?
3.
 What is the access to the system? Is it wide open or controlled? Are there w
ays 
to circumvent the process? Are there ways from authorized users in one part of 
the system to access the remainder of the system (even if they are not authorized 
in that area?) What types of commands and actions could they conduct? If this 
was possible, what would be the impact of the users? What if there were unin-
tentional, but still incorrect commands that users could execute – how would 
the system respond?
4.
 What is the physical protection of the system? 
Are there specific areas for the 
direct system control, maintenance access, or data repositories that may be 
available to anyone without proper authorization and access?
5.
 What is the state of the data that the system operates with? Are there proper 
safe
guards for data that resides at rest within the system? What about data 
security when it is in transit from one system to another?

ailable from open source or 
public areas of access? Are critical operational details available to anyone 
without proper access and need to know?
7.
 Are critical 
components of the system identified to employ additional protection 
capabilities? Are these components given adequate protection? Are there capa-
bilities to detect malicious activity, and if detected, are there adequate response 
features to be implemented? Are there sufficient recovery plans in the case of 
malicious action?
Critical Functional Analysis
The SSE engineer can evaluate the system operations through analysis of the functions 
and interfaces that the system performs. The SSE engineer may rely on their own 
security knowledge or need additional consultation on how the system may work to 
properly assess the criticality of the functions. Often, a functional decomposition will 
assist the SSE engineer to identify the critical functions that may have significant 
impacts on the entire system operations. Other views may require some analysis to 
determine if functions at critical phases in the system operations may adversely affect 
the overall performance. Operational analysis using degraded functions (in various 
phases of the functional flow) may also identify selected functions (or combinations of 
functions) that would need to be protected or hardened.
Critical Interface Analysis
As today’s systems are increasingly interconnected and require external interactions to 
successfully complete their objectives, the SSE engineer may also evaluate these critical 
=====PAGE 628=====
TYPES OF SECURITY  615
interfaces that inadvertently cause the system to fail or produce a less than desirable 
result. A sequence diagram to analyze the interfaces and sequence of interactions may 
identify critical junctures where dependencies on external systems may affect the 
systems overall performance. SysML models can be queried (for example, to find all 
uses of a signal or every interface on which it may be conveyed); these queries may be 
displayed in tabular or matrix form. Alternate interfaces or sources may be recom-
mended based on the criticality of interface or level of trust in the dependencies. 
Knowledge of how the system will react based on correct or incorrect data coming 
through the interface (or also the correct or incorrect interpretation of this data by the 
system operator) may provide insight into the level of importance to the system.
Access to the System
Many security professionals look at malicious outsiders attempting to enter the system, 
although the SSE also needs to consider the insider threat that is already inside and 
operating the system. Unrestricted access from any user may be perilous to system 
operations, if it was intentional or unintentional. The SSE engineer should consider all 
the different roles and users that will access the system, in what capacity and what level 
of access is possible from their role. Implementing protection such as role‐based access 
may help limit unnecessary access by other users that interact with the system. Moving 
laterally through the system (with an already authorized access point) may cause harm 
to the system. Evaluating how much access that the users (any types: operators, main-
tainers, testers, management, etc.) should be evaluated to determine how vulnerable the 
system is to the inside threat. Red teams are well versed in exploring the available 
access that is not visible to the decision makers.
System Physical Security
As much of the attention is paid to the cyber and data information security, the SSE engi-
neer should also consider the physical security status of the system and its supporting 
infrastructure. This may also provide additional access points for malicious threats and 
unwitting users to access the system and cause irreparable damage to the operations. Areas 
of importance to the system such as data centers, user terminals, or maintenance access 
ports are just a few areas that should have some physical security measures. Typically the 
areas inside of a security perimeter are left unlocked or open, presumably based on the 
assumption that the external protective barrier is sufficient, and are ripe for exploitation. 
The SSE should collaborate with the physical security officer to identify easily accessible 
areas within the system’s boundary (to also include partnering organizations and systems) 
in an effort to strengthen the areas that may be more susceptible to exploitation.
Data Security
Data security is important to the system operations, both at rest, in transit, and in use. 
Data at rest is typically stored in the system or in an external data storage system in the 
=====PAGE 629=====
616 SYSTEMS SECURITY ENGINEERING
form of databases, data warehouses, archives, tapes, backups, etc. If the data is not being 
used, it is considered at rest and should be protected from unauthorized handling, eval-
uation, or use. Data in transit is data that is being retrieved and transferred from one site 
to another. The SSE should reduce the possibility that this data could be intercepted or 
corrupted. Using network security solutions, data protection solutions, and encryption 
protocols may assist with the protection of this data. Finally, when the data is at the 
endpoint, users are able to interact with the data. Preventing unauthorized copying, 
manipulation, deletion, or other malicious activities should be the goal for the SSE. Use 
of strong user authentication, identity management, and profile permissions are examples 
of how security may be maintained. With any organization, a robust training program 
and continuous monitoring of the security can aid in a successful security program.
Operational Security
The system may have the best security practices, but letting someone discuss critical 
information to the outside world may nullify all of the security available. Ensuring that 
only authorized users that have a “need to know” will have access to the system’s criti-
cal functions and operations. Sometimes knowing about seemingly unrelated operations 
that are connected to the system operations can alert adversaries to find alternate paths 
to exploit the system, such as upcoming tests, or an increased dependency on services 
from other organizations. Evaluating the external footprint of the system during 
development and operations may also lend insight into the security of the program. 
Again, red teams can conduct open‐source intelligence by trolling the Internet or chat 
boards to determine if there are critical programs under development.
Security Framework
Having a proper framework to evaluate the program’s security may also provide 
guidance and proper application of resources to the program. The NIST Cybersecurity 
Framework (CSF) offers a basic framework that can be applied to any program to 
implement security. The first step is the “identify” phase to determine what the critical 
nodes are in the system that require some protection. The second step is to “protect” 
these critical nodes with the available protective technologies and methods. The third 
step is to “detect” and monitor for malicious activity against the system, with the 
defenses that were just installed. The fourth step, if the system is attacked, is to “defend” 
against the malicious efforts against the system and to repel any damage or activity. 
The fifth step, if the system has been damaged, is to “recover” to an acceptable state 
of operations and restore critical capabilities for users to continue system operations.
22.3 SECURITY APPLICATIONS TO  SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
SSE may be applied to different aspects of the systems engineering life cycle as the 
system concept is under development. The SSE engineer must interface with the rest 
of the SE team to develop the security requirements, identify security functions and 
=====PAGE 630=====
SECURITY APPLICATIONS TO SYSTEMS ENGINEERING  617
designs, develop the architecture that the system must implement, integrate the security 
capabilities during the development and integration cycle, and finally execute the secu-
rity testing during the installation and testing phases. Figure 22.2 is used to assist in 
identifying where SSE could be applied within the SE life cycle process.

understanding and documenting normal operations of the system, while other require-

“red team” members that intentionally seek out flaws and errors in systems in order to 
identify areas for improvement, while other inputs could be from making errors (inten-

from evaluation and study of other similar (or dissimilar) systems that may have been 
previously attacked and/or failed, so as to inspire additional security requirements. 
Study of the threat and how it evolves can also provide additional requirements.
Security Design and Integration
As the SSE engineer understands the security requirements that the system concept 
must perform, there will be options on how to execute these requirements with appli-
ances, applications, training, or skills that can help address these requirements. As the 
solution space is considered, equal consideration must be given to how these design 
solutions would integrate within the rest of the existing system (if it is being retrofitted 
for additional security), or the future system (if it is a new program) components. 
Going through use cases and scenarios to understand how the security appliances must 
work with the different parts of the software, hardware, or users can provide additional 
insight on what information and interfaces are needed to succeed in the use case. SSE 
integration may also need to consider other trade space within the system concept and 
may need to adjust the design performance based on other decisions made for the final 
system design.
Security Testing
During the testing phase, SSE engineers will also need to ensure the system concept 
has the proper testing of the security capabilities, in addition to the conventional system 
performance testing. Coordination between the security and non‐security testing will 
need to occur in order to minimize duplication of testing resources and maximize cov-
erage of testing objectives. As mentioned in the requirements phase, there may need 
the use of the red team that understands the threat concepts and tactics in order to test 
the system under realistic conditions and adversary capability. Equally important to the 
system testing is the understanding of the systems condition when under security testing 
and to evaluate whether the user can comprehend the system status and maintain situ-
ational awareness while the system may be compromised. This may be challenging to 
adequately test this comprehension if the system status is not readily apparent or pro-
vides a visible status change.
Security in the Supply Chain
Not only will the system be evaluated during the operations but also during the sustain-
ment phase through the supply chain, as faulty spare parts and updates may cause the 
=====PAGE 632=====
SECURITY APPLICATIONS TO DOMAINS  619
system performance to degrade. Other issues with a corrupted supply chain could have 
the fault remain dormant until a critical operation or command is needed. Sufficient 
measures should be evaluated while the system is undergoing periodic maintenance as 
well as longer‐term upgrades and improvements.
Security in the Operations and Maintenance Phase
While the system is in operation (and being maintained to ensure the system is readily 
available when needed), the SSE engineer would be interested in ensuring that proper 
security is maintained during these phases. This may include operational security 
regarding the deployment plans or operational techniques that the system will employ. 
This may include physical security on the actual system, support components, facilities, 
and personnel (operators and suppliers) that work to service the system, which may 
include third‐party vendors and foreign country support organizations. Public release 
of information that could provide valuable insight into the system capabilities and lim-
itations should also be checked to make sure that inadvertent disclosure of this 
information is not provided.
Security in the Disposal Phase
Once the system is ready for disposal, the SSE engineer must ensure that residual 
information, data, or technology does not exist that any scavengers can extract from 
the system once disposed. This may mean the use of clearing and destroying the 
memory from information systems, physical components that can provide valuable 
intelligence or corporate/manufacturing secrets that could be replicated, documentation 
regarding operations and maintenance procedures, or personnel that need to be debriefed 
and encouraged not to divulge proprietary or classified information.
22.4 SECURITY APPLICATIONS TO  DOMAINS
There are numerous applications of SSE that can be applied to different domains. 
Included are several representative examples of different domains and how SSE could 
be influencing the SE life cycle. Figure 22.3 provides some areas for where SSE could be 
overlaid onto other domains requiring systems engineering.
Defense/Homeland Security
Defense systems rely on security measures in order to protect critical and proprietary 
manufacturing formulas, unique operating capabilities, and maintaining their capa-
bility during the operational period. SSE engineers are keen to ensure that intruders 
are kept out of the system, as well as ensuring that the insider threat does not leak 
=====PAGE 633=====
620 SYSTEMS SECURITY ENGINEERING
information out either. Security issues may also be of concern when operating with 
partnering organizations and/or countries that may knowingly or inadvertently release 
sensitive information regarding the system.
Transportation
The SSE engineer looks to ensure that transportation systems (particularly public trans-
portation) are safe as well as efficient to serve their intended population. Ensuring that 
the systems work properly in light of operator/passenger attempts to cause the system 
to fail would also fall into the SSE engineer’s concerns. Complying with social as well 
as technical guidelines to ensure safe operations of the system is also key for a suc-
cessful transportation system.
Agriculture
The SSE engineer may also be concerned with agriculture system safety, to ensure that 
the system will perform as needed in a safe manner, both for the operators’ safety and 
for the products that are handled and produced in the agriculture domain. They may be 
concerned with the amount of fertilizer or other chemicals that may come into contact 
with the food products that are being developed and may be concerned that their system 
follows technical and agricultural regulations.

Critical Infrastructure
Similar to the transportation sector, there are other critical infrastructure sectors that 
the SSE engineer may be involved in to develop security requirements, integration, and 
testing of systems. Work with the appropriate government officials, users, regulatory 
bodies, and understanding of the environment that the system will work in is key to 
applying the relevant security capabilities within the system.
22.5 SECURITY VALIDA TION AND ANALYSIS
The SSE engineer must be versatile to acquire and develop complementary skills 
to the rest of the SE team in order to ensure the system concept has sufficient 
security capabilities during the development phase. This section identifies different 
skills that the SSE engineer may acquire to meaningfully contribute to the SE 
project. The SSE engineer would serve in a similar capacity as other members on the 
SE team, and they will focus on the security aspects of the system’s interfaces with 
external entities and organizations, as well as focusing on the internal security 
processing of the system itself.  This may require additional understanding of the 
external connections that the system has, to include permissions, access control, and 
rulesets for allowing or denying connections as malicious processes may originate 
from outside the system and be transmitted for infection.  The SSE engineer will also 
need to understand the internal systems and software processes that operate the 
system to ensure that malicious processes are not inadvertently activated based on 
the logics and security settings.  Understanding how certain systems processes may 
be affected by security measures is also key, an example being time-sensitive calcu-
lations or processing that may be slowed by security checking; the SSE should be 
judicious in their allocation of security measures so as to not adversely affect the 
systems operations.
The security testing and analysis performed by the SSE will also be key to ensuring 
that security controls and measures will not interfere or degrade the system operations; 
refer to the testing approaches described in chapter 17 to integrate with the SSE testing 
efforts.  SSE will also need to consider security updates to implement during system 
lifecycles, as security patches are regularly deployed based on security research as well 
as ad-hoc deployments based on outbreaks of malicious code that may infect a large 
amount of systems.  As many of the deployed systems are operating continuously, there 
may be little time or opportunity to take these systems off-line and update their security 
features, so a means of identifying and updating the entire portfolio of systems on a 
regular basis should be developed.

with other SE team members.

Systems Security Engineering

should take a holistic view of the system in order to identify what types of security 
may be needed to protect against threats.
Types of Security

is needed. Selected areas and questions may be posed to evaluate the systems 
security:
• Critical functional analysis
• Critical interface analysis
• Access to the system
• System physical security
• Data security
• Operational security
• Security framework

23.1 INTRODUCTION AND  MOTIVATION
This chapter concludes with a look toward the future of systems engineering (SE), how 
it has evolved, and where future systems engineers could look to ensure that the 
 profession remains a timely and relev
ant contribution to society.
We have seen how SE has matured from the aerospace and defense communities to many 
different domains, such as transportation, cybersecurity, healthcare, as well as incorporating 
different aspects such as human factors and software engineering. We look toward the future 
of SE to identify changes and disruptions, and seek to draw inspiration on why and how a 
systems engineer needs to continually adapt and grow in order to remain relevant.
Four changes are identified to help motivate these changes: change in user needs, 
system mission changes, competition and teaming changes, as well as the changing 
threat. Three disruptions may also cause the systems engineer to adapt in the environ-
ment and workplace: disruptions in technology, processes, and people–system inter -
faces. The successful systems engineer will look at disruptions as opportunities. Each 
of these areas is intended to identify where the systems engineer’s role can help to 
contribute to the challenges and advance the practice.
THE FUTURE OF SYSTEMS 
ENGINEERING
=====PAGE 640=====
628 THE FUTURE OF SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
User Needs Change
Some of the changes may be within the user needs themselves. As the user becomes 
more astute in learning the SE capabilities, and operating their legacy system in today’s 
environment, they may also look toward the future in determining their future spirals 
and version of their system in order to stay ahead of the competition, threats, and envi-
ronments. Other current events, such as climate change or conflicts, may necessitate a 
rapid change of capability that is needed by the system or introduction of new user 
communities and expertise that need a change in the existing system. The systems 
engineer would then need to elicit revised user needs and help to translate these 
new  needs into system and functional requirements in order to develop the new 
capabilities.
System Missions Change
Sometimes, current events may cause changes to the system in ways that it was not 
envisioned to originally operate in. As systems (typically military or space exploration 
ones) are inserted into the operational environment, these systems may not have been 
developed with this environment in mind, but the operators must accomplish their 
mission with the capabilities they were given. Sometimes, they will adapt the system 
in ways that the original designers and testers had not imagined which provides valuable 
lessons learned and insight into the next version of the system, particularly if it was 
successful in the field. Other times, the operators may discard the current system if it 
is not suited to their purpose. These system missions may mature over time and take 
on additional missions to remain relevant in the field. Military systems that are given 
additional missions over time include: air‐defense destroyers and cruisers will modify 
their original missions to take on land attack and ballistic missile defense roles to keep 
up with the emerging threats; similarly, air‐to‐air fighters will evolve to also take on 
the air‐to‐ground mission to remain a relevant contributor on the battlefield. The systems 
engineer would then have to evaluate how the existing system can still perform its 
original missions, as well as consider the new requirements, architecture, interfaces, 
and testing that would occur while affecting the new capabilities into the new system.
Competition and Teams Change
As the various systems evolve in their business operations, often their competitions will 
also change. Sometimes, these will be in the form of changing system development 
strategies in order to increase market share, or change the companies’ direction and 
attempt to capture business in a new area. These changes may introduce additional 
systems and capabilities that the stakeholders may be interested in, forcing their com-
petitors to consider adding these capabilities or creating new capabilities in response. 
These changes may also be in response to changes in the user and/or mission. 
The  systems engineer may need to elicit additional requirements, evaluate existing 
=====PAGE 641=====
INTRODUCTION AND MOTIVATION  629
requirements, or consider modification of the user needs and ultimate architecture 
while  considering how these changes would affect the current (and future) system 
configuration.
Teaming relationships may also emerge as a result in the change of environment, 
and former competitors may now become partners in certain proposals. Systems may 
need to change their interfaces and interpretation of data in order to interoperate with 
these new partners to enable the desired end results. Systems engineers should be well 
versed in describing these interfaces and enabling this knowledge transfer if this 
situation occurs.
Threats Change
Finally, the threats may change their behavior as well in response to the systems 
development and promise of future system performance. Through evaluation of the 
threats performance, the SE should be able to help analyze the current system, identify 
the gaps based on the desired outcomes, and help to derive new requirements and capa-
bilities to address these future threats. The SE will need to be more agile in this 
approach, as sometimes the intelligence picture of the threat is often vague and incom-
plete, so analysis without the full data may be needed. The timeframes in which to 
effect these changes may also need to be accelerated (again without the full threat 
knowledge) in order to stay ahead of the threat capabilities, and different design options 
or tradespace must be considered.
Technology Disruptions
Insertion of new technologies into society can quicken the pace of change required for 
users and industry to adapt to remain relevant. Increasing populations are much more 
readily accepting of new technologies. The common technology disruptor examples are 
the global positioning system (GPS) to provide precision location services and the 
Internet to provide global connectivity. Other disruptions are in the areas of energy 
sources, miniaturization, network evolution, and new material introduction. Systems 
engineers can help to envision the ways that new emerging technologies can augment 
existing user needs as well as elicit new needs. SE can also help to modify existing 
systems architectures to accommodate these new technologies and develop upgraded 
architectures as the new technology becomes more widespread.
Processes Disruptions
As governments, companies, and users find a different and innovative way of performing 
their objectives, eventually a shift of policies, procedures, and standards may need to 
be developed in order to help codify these processes. Before these procedures can be 
formalized, the SE may need to help find common definitions of these processes and 
assist users with the transition to the newer processes. The SE can help to conduct some 
=====PAGE 642=====
630 THE FUTURE OF SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
of the user needs cost/benefit analysis to show a legitimate case to switch processes. 
Other ways for SE to be involved is to test these processes to ensure that they are valid 
and can provide additional value.
People and System Interface Disruptions
Interaction between users and systems continues to evolve as newer systems are intro-
duced into society. A common example is the iPhone, with the unique (at the time) user 
interface and how it has affected a large portion of society to interact with the digital 
world. Other examples are the ride share programs to disrupt traditional taxi services. 
As new combinations of how users and systems interact and as newer services emerge, 
the SE can analyze how the impact to the user will change and help shape the newer 
requirements for different users. As this may also affect society at a larger scale than 
a single system, the SE may be called upon to perform holistic analysis on the greater 
society as newer systems are introduced.
23.2 AREAS TO APPL Y THE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING APPROACH
Future systems engineering efforts may be applied to different domains other than the 
traditional defense and aerospace projects. For some domains, a simple application of 
the SE life cycle model may be applied, while other domains may require a more 
holistic approach to adequately develop the system concepts. Even within traditional 
domains, the introduction of autonomous capabilities, intelligent networks, or global 
interfaces will require special attention. Listed below are selected domains (but not a 
comprehensive list) that could either benefit from systems engineering thinking and 
approaches or require techniques beyond the traditional SE approach.
Healthcare
Healthcare combines a variety of stakeholders, systems, and domains in order to 
 adequately capture the entire ecosphere that patients, physicians, nurses, and engineers 
need to contend with. Ne
w approaches with human–system interactions are providing 
healthcare services, some of which may be embedded within the patient in order to 
provide the data. New approaches may be needed for the SE to incorporate additional 
policies and standards when it comes to considering safety practices and requirements. 
Testing practices when it involves embedded systems may need to consider a different 
approach.
The healthcare domain also has a complex and interdependent ecosphere to include 
factors (to name a few) such as technology, insurance, government policies, hospitals, 
human factors, social factors, and home health care. Each factor has an influence on 
one or more factors when treating the patient, so a holistic SE perspective must be 
considered while developing the solution sets to address the stakeholders’ needs. Note 
that these interdependencies may differ when operating in different parts of the world, 
=====PAGE 643=====
AREAS TO APPLY THE SYSTEMS ENGINEERING APPROACH  631
so the SE must consider a tailored approach to systems development when serving the 
intended population. Global interactions and threats provide challenges and opportu-
nities to apply systems engineering practices to use technologies and services not 
 previously 
considered.
Transportation
Transportation will likely rely on both greenfield and brownfield SE approaches. 
A  greenfield SE approach can help identify unique transportation needs that require 
new infrastructure and new systems to provide the capability. A brownfield SE approach 
can help leverage existing infrastructure and provide an improved capability to integrate 
with the existing systems. In both cases, SE can help address transportation needs 
ranging from the most congested urban cities to the most remote rural areas. In addition, 
as transportation modes change, the systems engineer will need to not only think holisti-
cally but also be creative and accommodating change.
SE can help to synchronize the needs with the available infrastructure and 
 environment in order to balance the en
vironment and meet predicted future needs, 
potentially by leveraging existing natural landscape and areas if available. Systems 
engineers must also contend with resiliency and adaptation of system degradations in 
response to natural and man‐made disasters, when developing a robust system. When 
designing future systems, the SE should consider the wide range of users, services, and 
operating conditions. The future SE can help to define these conditions and develop 
new and existing systems to provide these desired levels of capability.
Environment and Critical Infrastructure
Multiple critical infrastructure (CI) sectors serve society, such as energy, water, com-
munications, finance, government, and transportation. Addressing problems at a larger 
scale (either a large region or country) to accommodate larger and growing problems 
will be challenges to SE to model, analyze, and test at a holistic, enterprise, and system 
of systems level. Incorporating the interdependencies between the various CI sectors 
can also help to model the problem, as well as apply systems thinking principles to 
discover the future required capabilities.
Understanding how a system will interact with both society and the environment 
will also be a challenge to the SE. Through systems thinking and complex adaptive 
systems analysis techniques, the SE can contribute to developing the enterprise‐wide 
capabilities.
Cybersecurity and the Internet of Things
Increasing the number of connected devices within society can help improve the quality 
of life for all citizens. However, the improvements in security must keep pace with the 
threats in order to ensure that the data are not corrupted and the original data intent is 
preserved. SE must also consider trust as an important factor when designing systems 
=====PAGE 644=====
632 THE FUTURE OF SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
to interoperate with humans, as well as ensuring that the systems making decisions are 
also considering system safety and security (e.g. physical, economic, and societal) when 
developing these systems. SE need to understand the divide between all human, all 
machine, and a blend of human–machine decision making, particularly as systems 
increase their edge computing (systems that will perform the calculations and actions) 
capability. With a large number of interdependent systems connected together that 
requires power and communications links, the SE will have challenges to define the 
changing requirements, architecture, and design at larger scales and faster deployment 
times.
Autonomous Systems
As advances continue in intelligent autonomous systems, their acceptance and com-
plexity will require comparable systems engineering development. Such systems 
include unmanned vehicles, robotics, aerospace systems (including drones), manufac-
turing development and assembly, human direct drug delivery, and financial trading 
systems. The methodical and thorough approaches of systems engineering is required 
for autonomous systems to address the complexity, social and ethical issues that arise 
during their development and operation. Autonomous systems can go where people 
can’t. They need to respond to unexpected, non-deterministic changes in the environ-
ment. Systems engineers will lead in concept to realization of these world changing 
systems. 
Manufacturing
The future SE can apply their contributions to manufacturing in order to keep up with 
increased and changing user demands. As users change their desires for a more tailored 
product to customize their user experience, the manufacturing organizations and 
systems must be more agile to adapt to these changes at speed and scale to meet the 
demand. As new products will need to interface with existing systems and be backward 
compatible, these systems will now need to accommodate additional complexity, inter-
faces, and data exchange. The use of transdisciplinary methods to consider the 
technical, societal, and user needs when developing a system will be a challenge to 
the SE team, particularly during the conceptual design, integration, testing, and deploy-
ment phases.
23.3 EDUCATION FOR THE FUTURE SYSTEMS ENGINEER
To stay ahead of the demand for improved SE products and services will require the 
SE education to be reevaluated to improve value to the existing SE education. The 
time‐tested concepts, processes, and approaches discussed in this book are the foundation 
all systems engineers should follow. Listed below are several topics to be explored to 
continue to produce quality SE products.
=====PAGE 645=====
EDUCATION FOR THE FUTURE SYSTEMS ENGINEER  633
Core Systems Engineering Topics
Systems engineers must maintain their competency in the core capabilities of problem 
definitions, requirements development, architecture construction, trade study analyses, 
and test and evaluation. Maintaining proficiency in systems engineering toolset(s) can 
help to interface with other customers and industry partners in order to contribute to 
SE product development and thinking. Toolsets are emphasized in order to expand the 
influence and compatibility of the engineer’s thinking, but does not replace the thinking 
of the systems engineer. Additional proficiency in advanced topics such as systems of 
systems and complex adaptive systems analysis can help with looking beyond a single 
system mentality.
Systems Thinking and a Holistic Perspective
Future SE can help develop a comprehensive approach toward systems development 
through greater use of systems thinking in a holistic perspective in order to look at 
interdependencies of the system. Considering different perspectives such as users, other 
systems, policies, cultures, or environments can provide the SE with a better under -
standing of the significant drivers of the system performance. This can lead to a series 
of richer requirements and can help the system become more resilient when faced with 
system degraded performance in situations such as disasters or obsolescence.
Transdisciplinary Development and Diverse Team Work
Systems engineers should be able to operate seamlessly within diverse teams in order 
to account for different users, perspectives, and needs. This teamwork can also build a 
robust set of requirements and assist in building comprehensive systems architecture to 
fully describe the needed functionality and interfaces. Incorporating different disci-
plines from a design perspective can provide additional insight into requirements and 
interfaces during the development.
Teamwork is especially critical with software‐intensive products and service systems. 
The SE must effectively incorporate software engineers and developers in the systems engi-
neering process, especially with the majority of future systems having software elements.
Model‐Based Systems Engineering and Digital Engineering
Developing systems within a MBSE environment can assist the SE team and the stake-
holders by providing a means to quickly visualize the products in modeling ecosystem 
rather than a document‐based static approach. This dynamic interaction of ideas and 
products can also help to shorten the SE life cycle duration, eliminate errors due to 
out‐of‐synch documents, and permit rapid impact analysis to support decision making. 
Being able to compare system alternatives and evaluate testing and maintenance pro-
cedures with a digital twin can help to anticipate issues before they emerge and help 
to prolong systems operations.
=====PAGE 646=====
634 THE FUTURE OF SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
Internet of Things and Complex Adaptive Systems Analysis
SE should be conversant with connected systems, devices, organizations, and users on 
a larger scale in order to consider how all of these objects may be expected to operate. 
As all of these independent objects operate and interact in the environment, different 
behaviors that were not planned or predicted during development may emerge, leaving 
the SE to assist in understanding and shaping the new behaviors and rules needed for 
system to successfully operate. By performing these complex systems analyses, the 
potential system of systems configurations can then be considered in order to develop 
informed analytical products to serve all systems operating in the ecosphere.
Education Beyond Traditional Modalities
SE must also consider education beyond the traditional formats, such as face to face, or 
online course modalities. Augmented reality and/or virtual reality technologies are two areas 
that may be considered to help expose the SE practitioners and students to see system oper-
ations in the perspective of the different stakeholders, thus gaining more insight into devel-
oping holistic and more realistic requirements. Global cooperation and collaboration that 
spans traditional academic boundaries may also become a new norm rather than an exception.
Agile Systems Engineering
Agile SE approaches may be considered as a new approach toward system development 
as opposed to traditional systems building, particularly as the user base and mission space 
becomes more flexible and demands more changes. As more systems become developed 
using this approach, the SE can help to shape the development and organization of effort 
and interoperability both within and external to the systems boundary. As the threats to 
the system may change their behavior as well (in response to the systems’ current and 
future system performance), an agile approach may be needed to quickly identify the 
relevant and nonrelevant parts of the system that must adapt to the new challenges.
23.4 CONCLUDING REMARKS
It is an exciting time to be a systems engineer. To see the progression of a single system 
development or system of system methodologies mature to handle the complex prob-
lems of the world should be inspiring systems engineers around the world. With the 
growing recognition of systems engineering as an academic field of study as well as a 
profession, SE can assist in many facets in today’s society from developing new and 
innovative capabilities, discovering where old concepts need new ideas, and integrating 
these new systems with legacy systems and natural environments when deployed. 
Welcome change. In fact, systems engineers can be the leaders of the future in the 
creation, development, and deployment of new systems. Good luck and think like a 
systems engineer!
=====PAGE 647=====
SUMMARY  635
23.5 SUMMARY
Introduction 
and Motivation
Systems engineers may need to adjust their thinking and adapt to a new problem set 
injected into society as a result of changes to the system or disruptive events.
Changes can include:
• Change in user needs
• System mission changes
• Competition and teaming changes
• Changing threat performance
Disruptions can include:
• Technology
• Processes
• People–system interfaces
Areas to Apply the SE Approach
The SE can apply the SE approach and adapt to new challenge to the subset of domains 
(not inclusive):
• Healthcare
• Transportation
• Environment
• Cyber and IoT
• Manufacturing
Education for the Future Systems Engineer
Systems engineers may need to reconsider the traditional modality of SE education. 
Some of these areas for consideration may include:
• Core SE topics
• Systems thinking
• Transdisciplinary of ideas
• MBSE and digital engineering
• IoT and complex adaptive systems
• Education beyond traditional modalities
• Agile systems engineering

636 THE FUTURE OF SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
PROBLEMS
23.1 State two projects within your organization that currently do not use systems 
engineering methodologies. 
Why not? What could you offer to assist these 
projects as a systems engineer?
23.2 Giv
en a new public transportation project that will be deployed in your home 
area. If there is no existing transportation system, what would you do to 
develop the concept? Who would you talk with? What thoughts would need 
to be elicited?
23.3
 If there is an existing transportation system, what w
ould you retain from the 
existing system while developing the new system? What would you do to 
integrate the two systems? Who would you consult? What testing approaches 
would you take?
23.4
 Giv
en an opportunity to clean a major international river, develop a 
systems approach to address the problem: clean the river water as well as 
providing clean drinking water to the residents near the river. Does the 
problem increase in complexity if the residential population is 1 million 
or 40 million?
23.5
 Giv
en the objective of cleaning the floating garbage ball in the Pacific Ocean, 
develop a systems thinking approach to address this issue. Identify the 
various organizations and systems that would need to interoperate to succeed. 
What are three main measures of success for this effort? How would you 
elicit these measures with the partnering organizations?
